Throughout history, if you were a fast growing company that needed real money, there was really only one place to find it.

When Amazon filed to go public in 1997, they said exactly this.

Congress passed a new law called the National Security's Markets Improvement Act.

Before 1996, a private investment fund, like the venture capital funds that back start -ups, could only have 100 investors, which means if you wanted to raise a billion dollar private investment fund, every one of those 100 investors had to bring an average of $10 million.

So during this time, private funds relied on a small number of ultra -wealthy individuals to write massive checks, which is why most private funds were smaller and why there just wasn't enough capital in the private markets to go around.

But this new law removed the 100 -person cap as long as every investor in the fund was what's called a qualified purchaser, which is an individual with at least five million dollars in investments or an institution with at least 25 million dollars.
This opened the door for institutional capital to flood into private markets.

It meant pension funds, university endowments, and other investors with deep pockets could now pour money into venture capital and over time hedge funds and even mutual funds started buying into startups, which meant the biggest pools of money in the world were now entering the private markets.

The same way a public company reports its financials, a private company would have to file quarterly reports, an annual report, and an update every time something big happened, which was a huge deal for startups because startups pay people in stock.
